title: Exxon Mobil Stocks Edge Lower as Brent Jumps 3.5% on Refinery Attack - TradingView
content: Exxon Mobil XOM shares edged lower by 0.09% to $158.08 at the 4:00 p.m. ET close on November 25, even as Brent crude settled up 3.5% at $94.61 a barrel after Yemen's Houthis said they attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery. West Texas Intermediate rose 2% to $83.68, after both benchmarks had gained more than 2% the day before. The impact on supply remains unclear. A person with knowledge of the matter confirmed to Reuters that the refinery came under attack, while the Saudi government and Aramco did not immediately comment. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a container ship near Hormuz was targeted and stopped on November 24. U.S. commercial crude inventories rose 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million in the week to November 20, and OPEC+ meets on November 29 to set 2027 output. Exxon's flat close against a 3.5% Brent jump suggests investors are treating the spike as a temporary risk premium, not a lasting supply shift. The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of 71/100, with a strong balance sheet and decent profitability but momentum near the bottom of GuruFocus's scale. GF Value of $146.93 puts the shares at a 7.6% premium and a "fairly valued" label, so investors are not paying extra for geopolitical upside. title: Your Exxon Dividend Needs Only About $59 Oil - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire? Oil has fallen, and oil stocks have fallen with it. WTI crude, the main U.S. oil price, fell 17.3% from $108.21 on Oct 16 to $89.53 on Nov 17. Exxon Mobil stock fell 14.4% in the month to Monday’s close. Chevron fell 11.6%. So what oil price do their payouts actually need? On each company’s own record since 2015, Exxon’s dividend and share buybacks together need WTI to average about $79 a barrel over a year. Chevron’s need about $80. The dividend alone needs much less. That line is about $59 for Exxon and about $65 for Chevron. Oil’s latest print is 12.9% above Exxon’s full-payout line. It is 11.3% above Chevron’s. On this measure, both payouts are still covered. Our read is that the dividends are the safe part, and the buybacks are what cheaper oil would test. Free cash flow is the cash a company keeps after paying for its wells, plants and other capital spending. In the four quarters to September, oil averaged $78.87 a barrel. That is close to the full-payout lines above, about $79 for Exxon and $80 for Chevron. In those months, Exxon’s free cash flow covered its dividend 2.5 times. Its dividends plus buybacks used 87.9% of free cash flow. Chevron’s payouts used 73.3%. Exxon Mobil’s cash covered its quarterly checks to holders 2.5 times over the past year, even as the stock fell 14.4% in a month. If those checks pay your bills, the falling share price is the part you have to sit through. EOG Resources covered its dividend 3.4 times, the widest margin in the group. The Energy Select Sector SPDR fund, which holds many of these names, fell 13.6% over the same month. The wider market did not drive Monday’s selling. The SPDR S&P 500 fund rose 4.7% that day, while Exxon fell 1.9%. We set each company’s free cash flow for every calendar year from 2015 to 2025 against that year’s average WTI price. A straight line fits Exxon’s record closely. Each $1 a barrel was worth about $1 billion of Exxon’s yearly free cash flow. For Chevron, each $1 was worth about $714 million. We then found the yearly oil price at which that cash equals the latest twelve months of payouts. A check on 47 single quarters gives nearly the same lines. It puts Exxon’s full-payout line at $78.34 and Chevron’s at $78.08. Today’s companies did better than the old record predicts. At the past four quarters’ $78.87 oil, the fit expected $37.3 billion of free cash flow from Exxon. Exxon produced $43 billion. The fit expected $23.9 billion from Chevron, and Chevron produced $34.1 billion. So the lines above are, if anything, on the high side. For how large Exxon’s cash is next to its share price, see Should You Buy Exxon Mobil Stock For Its Cash? For the same test on Chevron, see Should You Buy Chevron Stock For Its Cash? The twelve-month average hides when the cash arrived. 82.6% of Exxon’s free cash flow came in the April to September quarters. For Chevron the share was 88.3%. Oil averaged $95.65 and $87.11 in those two quarters. A year earlier, oil averaged $68.17. At that price, Exxon’s dividends plus buybacks were 159.5% of its free cash flow. Chevron’s were 167.4%. The gap had to come from the balance sheet. From 2015 to 2025, Exxon’s cash covered its dividend in 7 of 11 years. It covered the full payout in only 5. Chevron covered its dividend in 7 years and the full payout in 4. Exxon raised its dividend per share 4% on its latest quarterly call. Management said that was its 44th straight year of growth in the dividend per share. Asked about buybacks at $60 oil, Exxon’s chief executive answered on the dividend. “We’re not going to ever cut our dividend,” he said. The buyback is less firm. Exxon plans to keep buybacks at $20 billion in 2027, “assuming reasonable market conditions”. Chevron said it has kept buybacks at a rate of $2.5 billion to $3 billion a quarter and intends to stay in that range. Two smaller producers state their own lines, measured differently from ours: The test is the yearly average, not one day’s print. So far this quarter, WTI has averaged $98.76, well above both lines. If oil instead averaged below about $80 for a year, we think buybacks would be the first thing to shrink. The dividends look safe on this record down to about $59 for Exxon and $65 for Chevron. Our read: the recent fall prices in more risk to the dividends than the cash shows. The buybacks are the part that needs oil to average above about $80.
